text:
Applicant has concluded from studies of Lake Jocassee (Appendix J, Exhibit W, Duke Power Company, 1976c), that there was an overall net loss of about 1 to 3 meters of optimum trout habitat (water under 20°C and with 5 mg/l or more DO) in the main body of the lake from 1974 to 1975, resulting from operation of the Jocassee station and natural causes, with about 12 meters of habitat remaining, during the critical period in 1975. Applicant also concluded that there is no indication that discharges from the Jocassee station into Lake Jocassee have eliminated thermal stratification in Lake Jocassee.
Staff believes that comparing the depth and thickness of habitat loss in Jocassee Reservoir for 1974 and 1975 does not fully explain the effect the operation of the Jocassee pumped storage plant, in conjunction with Lake Keowee, has on the reservoir habitat. The greatest impact on the coldwater layer during the stratified period would be caused by the cumulative effect over 3 to 4 months of the Jocassee Project's removing some cool water during the generating cycle and discharging warm water during the pumping cycle. In addition, the proposed Bad Creek Project would remove some cool water from the Jocassee Reservoir during the pumping cycle and discharge warm water during the generating cycle, thereby accelerating the removal of coldwater habitat.
The Oconee Nuclear Power Plant located on Lake Keowee operated at about an 80 percent plant factor during July through September 1975. Warming of Lake Keowee water by the Oconee Nuclear Plant contributed to temperatures being in excess of 20°C in the water pumped into Lake Jocassee. This warm water replaced about 311,000 acre-feet of the approximately 437,000 acre-feet (Table 2-10) of coldwater habitat for the July-September period 1975. The 311,000 acre-feet is about 81 percent of the approximately 384,000 acre-feet removed from the Jocassee Reservoir during the generating cycle for the period. Similar results occurred in 1974 when the Jocassee Project commenced power generation in early September. However, the volume of coldwater habitat removed was less because neither the Jocassee Project nor the Oconee Nuclear Plant were operating at high plant factors. Applicant proposes to generate at the Jocassee plant about 12 to 15 hours per day, 5 days a week, or to operate above a 30 percent plant factor.
Without power generation during the periods August to September 1973 and July to August 1974, there appears to have been only nominal or natural changes in warming of coldwater habitat in Jocassee Reservoir.
